<speak>She looked at the journal once more. The lines to every edge. The rendering of a signature too large for any page she could give it, being transcribed anyway, page after page, by a man who had waited two years for the medium and the person to arrive at the same time. She had not found the edge of it. She was no longer certain the edge existed, and she noticed that the uncertainty had stopped functioning as a deficit in the differential and started functioning as a finding. But she had the rendering. That was more than she had had yesterday, and yesterday's holdings had been more than the day before, and that was the shape of the whole admission, and possibly of the work itself.<break time="750ms"/>
"Good night, Ruan."<break time="400ms"/>
"Good night."<break time="400ms"/>
She left the door open a hand's width.<break time="550ms"/>
The corridor took her back through the west wing at its evening pitch, past the imaging bay junction where a quality had once stood at the edge of her range being careful, and the ward settled around her into its night configuration, the lights stepped down, the station lamp on, the building beginning the long quiet hold it kept until morning. At her office she did the last accounting, short, in its settled shape: account given, chart current, notes written, questions racked, patient fed and stable and present. She put the physical chart in her bag. Third night of a practice.<break time="750ms"/>
The repeater glowed on the desk. Five channels moved in their small honest ways. The sixth was blank, as it had been blank on Day 2 and Day 15 and Day 30 and this morning, and she read it the way she had finally learned to read it — not as a failure, because it was not a failure; it was a reading. The instrument was reporting, faithfully, the one thing it knew: that what it was pointed at lay outside its range. That was where he was. That was where the whole case was, and she was keeping it there, on paper, in pencil, in a rendering that did not end at the edge of the page.<break time="750ms"/>
She turned off the desk lamp, and the ward made its night sound — the low held note of a place at work — and the sixth channel kept its blank and patient watch over everything the instruments could not yet say, which was not nothing, which was, as of today, a frequency, transcribed and in her care, and not finished, because it was never going to be finished, because it had never been finished to begin with.<break time="750ms"/></speak>
